text: Meet SafetySense. It calls for help when you can't.
Start a Guard for a walk home, a night out, a date, or a ride. Tap it, press the Action Button, ask Siri, or use the Lock Screen.
While it's on, your phone listens for screams, breaking glass, distress words, and your safe word. It feels for a fall, then stillness. All the listening happens on your phone.
If something seems wrong, it asks quietly: You okay? You have 45 seconds. One tap if you're fine.
tts: If something seems wrong, it asks quietly: You okay? You have forty-five seconds. One tap if you're fine.

text: No answer? Your trusted contacts get an automated call, and a text with a live link.
They see your location, your battery, and a timeline. And they can tap: I'm on my way, or send help now.
Still no safety PIN after 90 seconds? Professional dispatch calls you. If you can't answer, they send police to your live location. In this demo, dispatch is simulated.

text: Your safety PIN stops it. Your duress PIN looks exactly the same, but quietly keeps help coming.
And if your phone is smashed or switched off mid-session, our server notices the missing heartbeat, and raises the alert by itself.
Need a way out? A fake call gives you a reason to leave.
It only listens when you turn it on. Audio stays on your phone. Nothing is saved unless an alert fires, and evidence is encrypted, behind Face ID.
On the phone, Apple's sound and speech models feed a rules-based risk engine. In the cloud, Supabase watches heartbeats, Twilio calls your people, and Noonlight handles dispatch.
SafetySense was built by George Teifel, an electrical engineering senior at UNM, and Mary Teifel, a mechanical engineering freshman at CNM.
